subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: An object is partly submerged in water. What causes the upthrust on it?
options: The object is lighter than air
The water pressure is greater on the bottom than on the top of the object
questions.explain: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth, so the upward pressure on the bottom of the object is greater than the downward pressure on its top. This difference produces a net upward force called upthrust.

questions.q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume is halved. According to pV = constant, the new pressure is...
questions.explain: At constant temperature pV is constant, so if V is halved, p must double to keep the product the same (Boyle's law).

questions.q: Which quantity is measured in a derived unit rather than an SI base unit?
questions.explain: A derived unit is built from base units. Speed (m/s) is metres divided by seconds, so it is derived. The second, metre and kilogram are SI base units.

questions.q: How do all electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum?
options: All at the same speed (the speed of light)
Only visible light can travel through a vacuum
They cannot travel through a vacuum
At different speeds depending on frequency
questions.explain: All EM waves are transverse and travel at the same speed (about 3 × 10⁸ m/s) through a vacuum. They differ in frequency and wavelength, not speed in a vacuum.

questions.q: Which of these quantities is a scalar?
questions.explain: A scalar has magnitude only. Distance is a scalar; force, displacement and acceleration all have direction, so they are vectors. (Distance vs displacement is a common trap.)

questions.q: What is the difference between the mass and the weight of an object?
options: Mass is the amount of matter (kg); weight is the gravitational force on it (N)
Weight never changes but mass depends on location
Mass and weight are the same thing
Mass is measured in newtons; weight in kilograms
questions.explain: Mass is the amount of matter (in kg) and is constant. Weight is the gravitational force on that mass (in N) and depends on the gravitational field strength, so it changes between the Earth and the Moon.

questions.q: An object has a resultant force of zero acting on it. What can you conclude?
options: It is either stationary or moving at constant velocity
questions.explain: Zero resultant force means no acceleration, so the object stays still or keeps moving at constant velocity (Newton's first law).

questions.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
questions.explain: A vector has both magnitude and direction. Velocity has direction, so it is a vector; mass, temperature and speed are scalars (magnitude only).

questions.q: As you go deeper into a liquid, what happens to the pressure?
questions.explain: Pressure in a fluid increases with depth because there is a greater weight of fluid above pushing down (p = hρg).

questions.q: What does it mean if a spring is stretched beyond its limit of proportionality?
options: No more force is needed to stretch it
The extension is no longer directly proportional to the force
questions.explain: Beyond the limit of proportionality the force–extension graph is no longer a straight line, so extension is no longer directly proportional to force (and deformation may become inelastic).

questions.q: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease as you go higher up a mountain?
options: There is less air (a shorter column of air) above you pressing down
questions.explain: Atmospheric pressure is caused by the weight of the air above. Higher up, there is less air above you and it is less dense, so the pressure is lower.

questions.q: On a free-body diagram of a book resting on a table, which two forces are shown acting on the book?
options: Weight downward and the normal contact (reaction) force upward
questions.explain: The book's weight acts downward and the table pushes up with an equal normal contact (reaction) force. As they balance, the resultant force is zero and the book stays still.

questions.q: On a distance–time graph, what does the gradient (slope) of the line represent?
questions.explain: On a distance–time graph the gradient equals distance ÷ time, which is the speed. A steeper line means a faster speed.

questions.q: On a force–extension graph for a spring obeying Hooke's law, the line is:
options: A straight line through the origin
questions.explain: While a spring obeys Hooke's law, force is directly proportional to extension, so the force–extension graph is a straight line through the origin. The gradient equals the spring constant k.

questions.q: What happens to atmospheric pressure as you climb to a higher altitude?
questions.explain: As altitude increases there is less air above you, so the weight pressing down is smaller and atmospheric pressure decreases.

questions.q: An object floats when the upthrust acting on it is:
questions.explain: When floating, the upthrust (upward force from the fluid) balances the object's weight, so the resultant force is zero. If weight exceeds the maximum upthrust, the object sinks.

questions.q: A spring returns exactly to its original length after a stretching force is removed. This deformation is described as:
questions.explain: Elastic deformation means the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed. If it stays deformed, the deformation is inelastic (plastic).

questions.q: Why does light bend (refract) when it passes from air into glass?
options: Its speed changes, which changes its direction (unless it hits the boundary along the normal)
It speeds up in the glass
questions.explain: Refraction happens because the wave changes speed when it enters a different medium. Light slows down in glass; if it meets the boundary at an angle, this change of speed bends it toward the normal.

questions.q: What is the difference between elastic and inelastic deformation?
options: Elastic deformation returns to the original shape when the force is removed; inelastic does not
Elastic deformation is permanent; inelastic returns to shape
questions.explain: In elastic deformation the object returns to its original shape once the force is removed. In inelastic (plastic) deformation it does not fully return — it is permanently changed.

questions.q: What keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun?
options: The gravitational force of attraction from the Sun
questions.explain: Gravity provides the force that keeps planets in orbit. The Sun's large mass produces a gravitational attraction acting on each planet.

questions.q: In the required practical, how can you measure the speed of waves in a ripple tank?
options: Measure the frequency and wavelength, then use v = fλ
Time how long the tank takes to fill
Measure only the depth of water
Measure the amplitude and double it
questions.explain: You find the frequency (e.g. from the wave generator or by counting waves per second) and the wavelength (e.g. from a stroboscope or by measuring several waves), then calculate v = fλ.

questions.q: For an object in a circular orbit, in which direction does the gravitational force act?
options: Away from the centre of the orbit
Towards the centre of the orbit, acting as the centripetal force
There is no force on an orbiting object
questions.explain: Gravity acts towards the centre of the orbit, providing the centripetal force that keeps the object moving in a circle and constantly changing direction.
